name: World Politics
description: A core course examining the actors, structures, and dynamics of international relations, from state power and sovereignty to globalization, conflict, diplomacy, and contemporary global challenges.

modules.title: Introduction to International Relations
modules.objectives: Define international relations as a field of study; identify its core actors, levels of analysis, and major theoretical traditions; explain why world politics matters for everyday life.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax §14.4 is not assigned because its nuclear-law and preventive-action summaries are inaccurate. Required course instruction: IR examines cross-border interactions among states, intergovernmental organizations formed by governments, and nongovernmental actors such as aid NGOs or firms. Individual analysis examines a leader's beliefs; domestic/state analysis examines institutions, groups and political pressures within a state; systemic analysis examines anarchy (no overarching world government) and the distribution of power. One, two or several major power centers are called unipolar, bipolar or multipolar. Example: a flood response can be studied through a leader's choice, a legislature's funding rules, or interstate cooperation constraints. These lenses can interact; an observation at one level does not prove a complete explanation. International organizations have limited but real preventive tools: UN Charter Article 34 permits Security Council investigation of disputes or situations that may endanger peace, and Article 99 permits the Secretary-General to bring a threatening matter to the Council's attention. Mediation, envoys and political missions can be used before violence, but authority, cooperation and success vary; preventive capacity is not a guarantee. Required official texts: https://legal.un.org/repertory/art34.shtml and https://legal.un.org/repertory/art99.shtml .

modules.title: Nation-States & Sovereignty
modules.objectives: Define the nation-state and explain the origins of the modern state system; distinguish between nation, state, and nation-state; describe the concept of sovereignty and how it is challenged today.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax §14.3 is not assigned because its anarchy, enforcement and JCPOA summaries are inaccurate. Required official sources: UN Charter Article 2 at https://legal.un.org/repertory/art2.shtml ; Articles 39, 41 and 42 at https://legal.un.org/repertory/art39.shtml , https://legal.un.org/repertory/art41.shtml and https://legal.un.org/repertory/art42.shtml ; and the archived JCPOA implementation account at https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/issues/foreign-policy/iran-deal . Required concepts: a nation is a community of shared identity; a state is a political/legal entity; a nation-state is an idealized alignment of the two, not a claim of cultural uniformity. Montevideo's commonly cited criteria are permanent population, defined territory, government and capacity for international relations; recognition is a related but distinct political/legal issue. Sovereignty describes territorial authority and external independence within applicable international law, not exemption from obligations. Westphalia (1648) is a conventional historical marker, not the instant creation of all modern sovereign rules. Self-determination can create tension with territorial integrity, but does not automatically establish a general right of secession. In IR, anarchy means the absence of a central world government with a monopoly comparable to a domestic sovereign; it does not mean no order, rules or cooperation. International law and institutions can shape behavior. Enforcement is limited and politically conditioned, not nonexistent: under the Charter the Security Council may determine a threat under Article 39, authorize non-force measures such as sanctions under Article 41, and, under Article 42's conditions, authorize force. Vetoes, consent, capacity and noncompliance can restrict results. Historical distinction: Obama left office on 20 January 2017. JCPOA IAEA verification and Implementation Day occurred on 16 January 2016; verification, sanctions measures, treaty form and later political compliance are distinct questions.

modules.title: Realism & Liberalism in IR
modules.objectives: Summarize realist and liberal theoretical frameworks in international relations; compare their assumptions about human nature, state behavior, and the international system; apply each theory to a historical case.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax §§14.5–14.6 and the Stanford Encyclopedia overview §3.2 are not assigned because their summaries misstate realist-theory assumptions; the Stanford passage specifically attributes rational goal pursuit to Waltz, who did not require a rational-actor assumption. Read Mearsheimer, ‘Reckless States and Realism,’ pp. 241–242, at the linked URL for the Waltz/rationality distinction, then use this required course comparison. Realism is a family of approaches, not one universal rational-actor model. Classical realism, associated with writers such as Morgenthau, often emphasizes power, prudence and human/political motives. Structural realism explains constraints and incentives through anarchy and the distribution of capabilities; it does not require states or leaders to be rational or to reason perfectly. Defensive realist accounts emphasize that excessive expansion can provoke balancing and reduce security. Offensive realism explains why great powers under anarchy and uncertainty may seek opportunities to maximize relative power when expected benefits exceed risks and costs; it does not posit an intrinsic psychological drive for supremacy or claim conflict is inherently beneficial. Liberal institutionalism emphasizes rules, information, monitoring and repeated cooperation, with trade and domestic institutions also relevant to liberal accounts. Democratic peace is a qualified pattern of rare war between established democracies, not proof democracies never fight. Constructivism examines how interaction, identities and shared norms shape interests. Soft power uses attraction rather than coercion; a favorable cultural image is an example, but popularity alone does not prove a policy effect. Apply theories as lenses with assumptions and limits rather than universal laws.

modules.title: International Organizations (UN, NATO, WTO)
modules.titleZh: 国际组织：联合国、北约与世贸组织
modules.objectives: Describe the structure and purpose of major international organizations (UN, NATO, WTO, IMF); explain how intergovernmental organizations shape state behavior; assess both the capabilities and limitations of these bodies.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax §15.3 is not assigned because its UN founding/trusteeship, veto and WTO membership summaries are inaccurate. Required official sources: the free Charter texts at https://legal.un.org/repertory/art24.shtml , https://legal.un.org/repertory/art25.shtml and https://legal.un.org/repertory/art27.shtml . Correction: P5 members cannot veto every Council action. Procedural decisions require nine affirmative votes and are not subject to a permanent-member veto; substantive decisions also require no P5 negative vote under Council practice, while abstention does not itself veto. Article 24 in Chapter V assigns primary peace-and-security responsibility; Article 25 concerns carrying out Council decisions under the Charter. Do not call every resolution or recommendation binding without examining its terms and authority. NATO is a collective-defense alliance: Article 5 treats a covered armed attack on one as an attack on all, with each ally taking assistance it deems necessary, not automatic identical military action. Official text and explanation: https://nato.int/en/what-we-do/introduction-to-nato/collective-defence-and-article-5 . WTO members negotiate trade rules and use dispute procedures; the IMF addresses monetary/balance-of-payments needs; the World Bank provides development financing. WTO limitation: its Appellate Body cannot hear appeals because of vacancies (checked November 2026); this does not mean all dispute procedures have ceased. Official explanation: https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dispu_e/appellate_body_e.htm . Membership correction: exclude §15.3’s undated statement that the WTO has 164 members. The WTO official page reports 166 members after the 30 August 2024 accessions; membership can change and the exact count is not assessed. Direct evidence: https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/who_we_are_e.htm . UN chronology correction: the United Nations officially came into existence on 24 October 1945, not 1946. The eleven Trust Territories reached self-government or independence through different outcomes, including independence, free association or joining an independent state; do not say every territory followed the same independence path. Official overview: https://www.un.org/en/about-us/trusteeship-council .

modules.title: Globalization
modules.objectives: Define globalization and describe its economic, cultural, and political dimensions; distinguish between hyperglobalists, skeptics, and transformationalists; evaluate the benefits and costs of globalization for different populations.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax §16.5 is not assigned because its crisis-policy and Bretton Woods summaries are inaccurate. Read the linked WTO institutional overview for one part of cross-border economic governance, then use this required course lesson on the three perspectives. Globalization connects production, markets, culture and governance across borders, with uneven gains and costs. Hyperglobalists emphasize historically transformative integration that erodes the significance of borders and state economic control. Skeptics challenge claims of an unprecedented borderless economy, emphasizing earlier integration, regional concentration and continuing state power; comparisons depend on the measure and period. Transformationalists emphasize deep but uneven changes in how state power is exercised, rather than inevitable disappearance or little change. Worked hypothetical: a state changes labor rules to attract a cross-border factory. A hyperglobalist highlights competitive market constraints; a skeptic highlights the state's continuing rule-making power; a transformationalist highlights changed governance across public and private actors. These are analytical emphases, not three proven outcomes. In the four-country assignment, a cheaper final device may benefit buyers while import competition harms some workers; distinguish possible effects from observed evidence.

modules.title: International Trade & Finance
modules.objectives: Explain comparative advantage and the rationale for free trade; describe key institutions of the global economy (WTO, IMF, World Bank); identify causes and consequences of trade disputes and currency crises.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax §16.5 is not assigned because its crisis-policy and Bretton Woods summaries are inaccurate. Required institutional sources: WTO overview at https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/who_we_are_e.htm ; IMF at-a-glance at https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/IMF-at-a-Glance ; and World Bank mission at https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/what-we-do . Use these with this required trade lesson. Comparative advantage means lower opportunity cost, not necessarily producing more with the same inputs. Example: in an hour A can make 2 units of cloth or 1 grain, while B can make 1 cloth or 1 grain. A's cloth costs 0.5 grain; B's costs 1 grain, so A has comparative advantage in cloth and B in grain. Potential aggregate gains from trade do not ensure every worker gains; adjustment and distribution matter. A tariff is an import tax, unlike an import ban, quota or exporter subsidy. Retaliation means a trading partner imposes a countermeasure, which can raise costs for different participants. IMF assistance addresses balance-of-payments pressures; World Bank financing focuses on development; WTO agreements and dispute processes concern trade rules. Economic sanctions restrict transactions to impose costs as a coercive tool, distinct from military force or attraction. Do not assume a tariff or sanction guarantees its intended result.

modules.title: Human Rights in Global Context
modules.objectives: Define human rights and trace the development of the international human rights regime; explain tensions between sovereignty and human rights intervention; evaluate the effectiveness of international human rights enforcement mechanisms.
modules.readingNote: Required sources and course instruction (OpenStax §15.2 is not assigned because its treaty and Geneva Convention summaries are inaccurate): read the OHCHR UDHR history at the linked page; the UN Genocide Convention history at https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/cppcg/cppcg.html ; Rome Statute Articles 6–7 at https://legal.un.org/icc/statute/99_corr/cstatute.htm ; and the ICRC Geneva Conventions overview at https://www.icrc.org/en/article/geneva-conventions-humanity-must-prevail . The UN General Assembly adopted the UDHR on 10 December 1948 as a declaration, not itself a treaty. The UDHR, ICCPR and ICESCR are commonly grouped as the International Bill of Human Rights. Universality means rights belong to people regardless of nationality or status; legal obligations and remedies still depend on applicable law. Do not conflate the nine core UN human-rights treaties with international criminal-law instruments: the Genocide Convention separately defines genocide and creates prevention/punishment obligations, while Rome Statute Articles 6 and 7 separately define genocide and crimes against humanity for ICC purposes. The four 1949 Geneva Conventions have distinct principal protections: I covers wounded and sick armed forces on land; II covers wounded, sick and shipwrecked armed forces at sea; III covers prisoners of war; IV covers civilians. They are not all limited to civilians and prisoners of war. Enforcement capacity is not the same as jurisdiction. The ICC considers individual responsibility for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression under distinct jurisdiction/admissibility conditions; it complements national proceedings and depends on state cooperation for arrests. Powerful-state status alone neither confers immunity nor establishes jurisdiction. R2P concerns genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity: states protect populations; international assistance and peaceful means come first; when peaceful means are inadequate and national authorities manifestly fail, collective coercive action is considered case by case through the Security Council under the Charter, not an unrestricted unilateral intervention right. Direct official evidence: https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n12/438/79/pdf/n1243879.pdf . Treaty process: signature does not universally create full binding participation. Under Vienna Convention Articles 11–14, consent to be bound may be expressed through signature only when the treaty or parties so provide; many treaties instead require ratification, acceptance, approval or accession. Article 18 supplies a narrower pre-entry duty not to defeat the treaty's object and purpose, pending the state's decision; full treaty obligations generally depend on valid consent and entry into force. For the Paris Agreement, use the UN depositary record to distinguish signature, later consent procedures and entry into force: https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetails.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=XXVII-7-d&chapter=27&clang=_en . Supplied non-graphic OHCHR digest (paraphrase, not quotation): representatives from varied legal and cultural backgrounds drafted the UDHR; the General Assembly adopted it in Paris in 1948 as a universal rights standard. This establishes adoption and aims, not that any government complied in practice.

modules.title: Causes of War & Conflict
modules.objectives: Identify and compare major theoretical explanations for war (realist, liberal, constructivist, domestic-level); distinguish between interstate and intrastate conflicts; explain why some disputes escalate to armed conflict while others do not.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax §§14.4 and 14.6 are not assigned because their nuclear-law, preventive-action and maritime-boundary summaries are inaccurate. Use this required conflict lesson and the official sources below. Interstate conflict is between states; intrastate conflict is principally within a state and may involve outside actors. A security dilemma occurs when defensive preparations are interpreted as threatening, prompting countermeasures even without an initial aggressive intent; escalation is possible, not inevitable. Domestic explanations examine institutions, interest groups and bureaucratic incentives; individual explanations examine leaders' beliefs and psychology. Diversionary-war theory proposes that leaders may seek external conflict to redirect domestic discontent; evidence is needed to distinguish it from other explanations. Constructivist accounts examine threat identities and norms; liberal accounts examine constraints and opportunities for cooperation. Collective action problems arise when individual incentives undermine shared goals; climate mitigation illustrates free riding because noncontributors can share benefits. No theory by itself proves why a particular war occurred. Nuclear-law distinction: permanent Security Council membership is not the legal test for nuclear-weapon possession. The NPT defines a nuclear-weapon state by manufacture and explosion before 1 January 1967 (Article IX); non-nuclear-weapon states parties undertake not to acquire weapons (Article II). India and Pakistan are not NPT parties. This does not settle every other applicable obligation; Charter use-of-force rules and treaty-party obligations are separate. Official NPT history/obligations: https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/tnpt/tnpt.html . Preventive-action distinction: Charter Articles 34 and 99 allow anticipatory investigation or attention to threats, and mediation/envoys/political missions may operate before violence. These tools have legal and practical limits and do not guarantee success. Official texts: https://legal.un.org/repertory/art34.shtml and https://legal.un.org/repertory/art99.shtml .

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following best defines 'international relations' as a field of study?
options: The study of local electoral behavior within municipalities
The study of interactions among states, international organizations, and non-state actors in the global arena
The study of constitutional structures within a single state
The study of individual personality development in isolation
quizQuestions.answer: The study of interactions among states, international organizations, and non-state actors in the global arena
quizQuestions.explanation: IR includes cross-border political, economic, security and cultural interactions. States, intergovernmental organizations and nongovernmental actors can all matter; a domestic-only field omits these interactions.

quizQuestions.question: The 'systemic level of analysis' in IR focuses on:
options: Domestic institutions and interest-group influence
Individual leaders' beliefs and risk perceptions
Bureaucratic rivalry inside a foreign ministry
The structure of the international system as a whole
quizQuestions.answer: The structure of the international system as a whole
quizQuestions.explanation: The systemic level examines how the anarchic structure of the international system and the distribution of power among states shapes behavior.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is an example of a non-state actor that plays a significant role in international relations?
options: Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders)
The Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
The United States Army
The French National Assembly
quizQuestions.answer: Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders)
quizQuestions.explanation: Doctors Without Borders is a nongovernmental organization rather than an organ of a national government. The other options are state institutions. Actor classification does not by itself establish an organization's effectiveness.

quizQuestions.question: Give one example of how international relations can affect everyday life and explain the cross-border connection.
quizQuestions.answer: For example, a cross-border shipping disruption can raise the cost of an imported good. Security, work, migration, rights or climate examples with an explicit connection are also acceptable.
quizQuestions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): a concrete everyday effect (0.5) and a causal cross-border link (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. A hypothetical example is sufficient; no personal experience is required.

quizQuestions.question: Which set lists the commonly cited Montevideo criteria for statehood, distinct from recognition by other states?
options: A permanent population, defined territory, effective government, and capacity to enter relations
Population, democratic elections, diplomatic recognition and a large military
Territory, a national currency, UN membership and a common language
Government, a shared religion, a trade surplus and formal recognition
quizQuestions.answer: A permanent population, defined territory, effective government, and capacity to enter relations
quizQuestions.explanation: The criteria concern population, territory, government and capacity for international relations. They are distinct from UN admission or a particular recognition decision; application to contested cases requires evidence and legal context.

quizQuestions.question: What does 'sovereignty' mean in international relations?
options: Military superiority over neighboring states
Recognition of a shared cultural identity across borders
Membership in an alliance with collective-defense obligations
Territorial governing authority and external independence within applicable international law
quizQuestions.answer: Territorial governing authority and external independence within applicable international law
quizQuestions.explanation: Sovereignty concerns authority and independence, not military dominance or freedom from every legal obligation. Treaty obligations, recognition and enforcement are related but distinct issues.

quizQuestions.question: A 'nation' in the IR sense refers primarily to:
options: An organization formed by agreement among governments
A territorial political entity with governing institutions
A group of people sharing common identity, culture, or history
A corporation operating in several national markets
quizQuestions.answer: A group of people sharing common identity, culture, or history
quizQuestions.explanation: A nation is a group bound by shared identity (language, culture, ethnicity, history), which may or may not have its own state — hence the distinction between nation and state.

quizQuestions.question: Which hypothetical event most directly raises a tension between non-intervention and international civilian protection?
options: A state issuing a new national currency
A state changing its domestic tax schedule
A state reforming its own electoral administration
The UN Security Council authorizing intervention in a state that has committed mass atrocities against its own citizens
quizQuestions.answer: The UN Security Council authorizing intervention in a state that has committed mass atrocities against its own citizens
quizQuestions.explanation: UN-authorized measures to protect civilians may limit a simple rule of non-intervention in a particular case. The legal authority and scope depend on the Security Council mandate; sovereignty does not disappear.

quizQuestions.question: Which assumption is central to the realist theory of international relations?
options: Domestic coalitions determine foreign policy preferences
The international system is anarchic and states prioritize survival and power
Norms and identities shape how states understand their interests
Institutions and interdependence can lower cooperation barriers
quizQuestions.answer: The international system is anarchic and states prioritize survival and power
quizQuestions.explanation: Realists argue the absence of a world government (anarchy) forces states to prioritize their own survival and power in a self-help system.

quizQuestions.question: Liberal theory in IR emphasizes that international cooperation is possible because:
options: State resources determine interests regardless of institutions
Institutions, interdependence and democratic constraints can reduce barriers to cooperation
Shared identities determine interests independently of formal rules
Military balancing provides the primary foundation of security
quizQuestions.answer: Institutions, interdependence and democratic constraints can reduce barriers to cooperation
quizQuestions.explanation: Liberal accounts examine mechanisms that can reduce uncertainty and incentives for conflict. These are qualified arguments about cooperation, not a guarantee that trade or democracy eliminates war.

quizQuestions.question: Hans Morgenthau is most associated with which theoretical tradition?
options: Marxism
Constructivism
Classical Realism
Liberalism
quizQuestions.answer: Classical Realism
quizQuestions.explanation: Morgenthau's Politics Among Nations (1948) is the foundational text of classical realism, arguing that states are driven by power and the national interest.

quizQuestions.question: Explain how a constructivist would understand state interests or identities, with one example.
quizQuestions.answer: Interests and identities are shaped through interaction and shared ideas or norms; for example, repeated cooperation can change how a neighbor is perceived. Equivalent clearly hypothetical examples are acceptable.
quizQuestions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): social shaping through norms, ideas or interaction (0.5) and a matching example (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. Material power need not be declared irrelevant.

quizQuestions.question: The United Nations was established primarily to:
options: Organize collective defense among a regional alliance's members
Promote international peace, security, human rights, and cooperation among states
Administer a specialized set of international trade agreements
Provide temporary financing for external-payment pressures
quizQuestions.answer: Promote international peace, security, human rights, and cooperation among states
quizQuestions.explanation: The UN Charter (1945) established the organization to maintain international peace and security, develop friendly relations among nations, and promote human rights and international cooperation.

quizQuestions.question: Which UN body has primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security?
options: International Court of Justice
UN General Assembly
UN Security Council
UN Secretariat
quizQuestions.answer: UN Security Council
quizQuestions.explanation: Article 24 in Chapter V assigns the Council primary responsibility for peace and security. Article 25 concerns members carrying out Council decisions in accordance with the Charter; legal effect depends on the relevant authority and decision, so not every statement or recommendation is categorically binding.

quizQuestions.question: In International Organizations (UN, NATO, WTO), NATO is best described as:
options: An institution providing balance-of-payments assistance
A North American and European collective-defense alliance
A court adjudicating individual responsibility for atrocity crimes
An organization administering negotiated trade agreements
quizQuestions.answer: A North American and European collective-defense alliance
quizQuestions.explanation: NATO is a collective-defense alliance. Under Article 5, a covered armed attack is treated as an attack on all, and each ally assists with action it deems necessary. This is not an automatic obligation to use identical military force.

quizQuestions.question: The World Trade Organization (WTO) primarily:
options: Hear individual criminal cases involving atrocity crimes
Provide balance-of-payments loans to member governments
Administer member-negotiated trade rules and dispute settlement procedures
Finance long-term development projects and technical assistance
quizQuestions.answer: Administer member-negotiated trade rules and dispute settlement procedures
quizQuestions.explanation: Members negotiate trade rules and use WTO dispute procedures. As checked in November 2026, vacancies prevent the Appellate Body from hearing appeals; the mandate should not be confused with fully functioning appellate capacity.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following best captures the meaning of 'globalization'?
options: Changes in government inside a state without external interaction
The increasing interconnection of economies, cultures, and politics across national borders
Growth in domestic production without cross-border connections
Expansion of one country's local markets within its existing borders
quizQuestions.answer: The increasing interconnection of economies, cultures, and politics across national borders
quizQuestions.explanation: Globalization refers to the accelerating integration of markets, cultures, technologies, and governance across national boundaries.

quizQuestions.question: 'Hyperglobalists' argue that globalization:
options: Is chiefly a domestic industrial policy rather than cross-border integration
Reshapes governance unevenly without necessarily eliminating state authority
Is creating a borderless global economy that is transforming or eroding state power
Mainly repeats earlier integration while states retain strong control
quizQuestions.answer: Is creating a borderless global economy that is transforming or eroding state power
quizQuestions.explanation: Hyperglobalists believe globalization is producing a qualitatively new global economy in which national borders matter much less than they once did.

quizQuestions.question: Which position best reflects globalization skeptics as defined in the required course note?
options: Market integration makes national borders economically irrelevant
Globalization necessarily ends state authority in every region
Current integration can be explained without any historical comparison
Claims of a borderless new era can be overstated because historical integration and state power still matter
quizQuestions.answer: Claims of a borderless new era can be overstated because historical integration and state power still matter
quizQuestions.explanation: Skeptics question claims of unprecedented borderlessness, pointing to earlier integration, regional concentration and state regulation. A comparison of integration across eras depends on the measure, so no universal quantitative equality is asserted.

quizQuestions.question: Which group is most directly exposed to job losses when lower-priced imports displace its industry's output?
options: Export-sector professionals in developing economies
Consumers in high-income countries buying imported goods
Low-skilled workers in industries exposed to low-wage import competition
Multinational corporations with globally diversified production
quizQuestions.answer: Low-skilled workers in industries exposed to low-wage import competition
quizQuestions.explanation: Workers in the directly competing industry can face displacement or wage pressure. Exporters and buyers can face different effects; actual outcomes depend on sector, institutions and adjustment, not skill labels alone.

quizQuestions.question: The principle of 'comparative advantage' in international trade argues that:
options: Countries should specialize according to the value of past imports alone
Countries should specialize according to absolute output per worker alone
Countries should specialize according to total market size alone
Specialization at relatively lower opportunity cost can create potential gains from trade
quizQuestions.answer: Specialization at relatively lower opportunity cost can create potential gains from trade
quizQuestions.explanation: Opportunity cost measures the alternative output forgone. In the required example, A gives up 0.5 grain per cloth while B gives up 1 grain, so A has comparative advantage in cloth. Potential total gains do not guarantee every participant gains.

quizQuestions.question: Which institution provides financing to member countries facing balance-of-payments problems?
options: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
World Bank
World Trade Organization
OECD
quizQuestions.answer: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
quizQuestions.explanation: The IMF addresses external-payment and monetary pressures. Its financing can have different terms and durations; the World Bank's development focus and the WTO's trade-rule role are distinct.

quizQuestions.question: An import tariff is best defined as:
options: A government tax on imported goods
A payment supporting domestic exporters
A quantitative ceiling on imported goods
A prohibition on imports of a specified good
quizQuestions.answer: A government tax on imported goods
quizQuestions.explanation: An import tariff taxes imported goods, unlike a quantity limit, prohibition or exporter subsidy. Its effect on final prices and on different groups depends on market conditions and responses.

quizQuestions.question: The World Bank's primary purpose, as distinct from the IMF, is to:
options: Coordinate exchange rate policies among major economies
Set global trade rules and adjudicate disputes
Provide long-term development financing and technical assistance to reduce poverty
Provide short-term emergency loans to stabilize currencies
quizQuestions.answer: Provide long-term development financing and technical assistance to reduce poverty
quizQuestions.explanation: The World Bank focuses on development financing and assistance, such as infrastructure or education projects. The IMF addresses balance-of-payments needs with financing of varying durations; it is not simply a development-project bank.

quizQuestions.question: In a hypothetical trade dispute, explain a tariff and a retaliatory tariff.
quizQuestions.answer: A tariff is a tax on imports. A retaliatory tariff is an import tax imposed by the trading partner in response to the first measure.
quizQuestions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): define the import tax (0.5) and identify the partner's responsive counter-tariff (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. Accept equivalent hypothetical goods and countries; no current-event claim is required.

quizQuestions.question: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted by the UN General Assembly in:
quizQuestions.explanation: The UDHR was adopted on December 10, 1948, and established a common standard of fundamental human rights for all peoples and nations.

quizQuestions.question: Human rights are described as 'universal' because:
options: They belong to all human beings regardless of nationality, ethnicity, religion, or other status
They arise from membership in a regional organization
They depend on a person's economic contribution
They arise from citizenship in a particular state
quizQuestions.answer: They belong to all human beings regardless of nationality, ethnicity, religion, or other status
quizQuestions.explanation: The universality principle holds that human rights apply to every person simply by virtue of being human, not contingent on citizenship or government approval.

quizQuestions.question: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), together with the UDHR, form:
options: The Rome Statute framework for international criminal responsibility
The Geneva Conventions framework for armed conflict
The UN Charter framework for collective security
The International Bill of Human Rights
quizQuestions.answer: The International Bill of Human Rights
quizQuestions.explanation: The UDHR (1948) plus the ICCPR and ICESCR (both 1966) are collectively called the 'International Bill of Human Rights,' constituting the foundational framework of the international human rights regime.

quizQuestions.question: Explain one practical obstacle to international human-rights enforcement and distinguish it from legal jurisdiction.
quizQuestions.answer: A court may depend on national authorities to make an arrest even when legal jurisdiction exists. Cooperation and political will can obstruct enforcement; jurisdiction is the separate question of legal competence.
quizQuestions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): a practical obstacle such as noncooperation or limited capacity (0.5), plus a correct distinction from legal competence (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. Powerful-state status alone does not remove jurisdiction.

quizQuestions.question: Which theoretical perspective would most emphasize the security dilemma as a cause of war?
options: Realism
Domestic bureaucratic politics
Constructivism
Liberal institutionalism
quizQuestions.answer: Realism
quizQuestions.explanation: Realists argue the security dilemma — where one state's defensive buildup makes others feel less secure, triggering arms races — is a structural cause of conflict inherent in anarchy.

quizQuestions.question: An 'intrastate conflict' is one that occurs:
options: Between governments over an international boundary
Between several sovereign states in opposing alliances
Within the borders of a single state (civil war)
Between the armed forces of two sovereign states
quizQuestions.answer: Within the borders of a single state (civil war)
quizQuestions.explanation: Intrastate conflicts (civil wars, insurgencies) occur within a country's borders, often between a government and non-state armed groups, as opposed to interstate wars between countries.

quizQuestions.question: The 'diversionary war' theory suggests that leaders may use military conflict to:
options: Secure access to natural resources
Distract the public from domestic political problems and rally national support
Fulfill treaty obligations
Balance power against a rising rival
quizQuestions.answer: Distract the public from domestic political problems and rally national support
quizQuestions.explanation: Diversionary war theory holds that leaders facing domestic unrest or declining popularity may initiate external conflict to boost nationalist sentiment and deflect attention from internal problems.

quizQuestions.question: Which domestic-level factors could help explain a state's decision to use force?
options: Regime institutions, interest-group pressure and bureaucratic incentives
A leader's personal risk perception considered alone
The international distribution of military power
The absence of a world government
quizQuestions.answer: Regime institutions, interest-group pressure and bureaucratic incentives
quizQuestions.explanation: Domestic analysis examines institutions and organized interests within states. Leader psychology belongs to the individual level; anarchy and interstate power distribution are systemic. These levels can interact.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines the field of international relations?
options: Study of individual personality development without social context
Study of voting behavior within a city
Study of interactions among states and non-state actors in the global arena
Study of constitutional organization inside a single state
questions.answer: Study of interactions among states and non-state actors in the global arena
questions.explanation: IR examines political, economic, security, and cultural interactions among states, international organizations, and non-state actors across national borders.

questions.question: Why is the Peace of Westphalia (1648) often discussed in IR courses?
options: It replaced territorial rulers with an international parliament
It codified the Montevideo criteria for diplomatic recognition
It established the modern UN Charter's collective-security machinery
It is a conventional historical marker in accounts of territorial authority and state sovereignty
questions.answer: It is a conventional historical marker in accounts of territorial authority and state sovereignty
questions.explanation: Westphalia ended major European wars and is often used as a marker in histories of sovereignty. Modern state rules evolved over time; they were not all created instantly in 1648.

questions.question: The four Montevideo criteria for statehood include permanent population, defined territory, effective government, and:
options: Membership in the United Nations
A common national language
Recognition by every neighboring state
Capacity to enter into relations with other states
questions.answer: Capacity to enter into relations with other states
questions.explanation: The Montevideo Convention (1933) defines statehood by these four criteria, the last being the capacity to conduct international relations.

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement? Realism in IR assumes that the international system is characterized by:
options: Anarchy, state self-help, and competition for power or security
Institutional rules and shared interests as a primary basis of cooperation
Socially formed identities as the source of state interests
Domestic interest groups as the central cause of external behavior
questions.answer: Anarchy, state self-help, and competition for power or security
questions.explanation: For realism, no overarching world government guarantees protection, so states face incentives for self-help and attention to relative power. This does not mean every realist predicts constant war.

questions.question: Liberal IR theory emphasizes which of the following as a source of international peace?
options: Military balancing and deterrence
Economic interdependence, democracy, and international institutions
Diversion of public attention from domestic problems
Threat perceptions formed through shared identities
questions.answer: Economic interdependence, democracy, and international institutions
questions.explanation: Liberals argue that trade, democratic governance, and institutions create shared interests and reduce the incentive for conflict.

questions.question: The UN Security Council's five permanent members each possess:
options: An extra vote on each substantive resolution
Veto power over substantive resolutions
Power to block procedural decisions even with nine affirmative votes
Exclusive authority to propose all Council resolutions
questions.answer: Veto power over substantive resolutions
questions.explanation: A negative vote by a permanent member can block a substantive Council decision. Procedural decisions are not subject to that veto; a permanent-member abstention does not itself block adoption under Council practice.

questions.question: State NATO's Article 5 collective-defense principle and explain one limit on what assistance it requires.
questions.answer: A covered armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all. Each ally takes action it deems necessary to assist; identical or automatic military action is not prescribed.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): attack-on-one/attack-on-all principle (0.5) and assistance determined by each ally rather than automatic identical force (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. Equivalent phrasing is accepted.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the skeptic perspective taught in the required globalization note?
options: Market integration has made borders and state regulation irrelevant
Globalization changes authority profoundly but unevenly without erasing states
Globalization is often overstated and states remain powerful actors
Cross-border connections are explained chiefly by domestic events alone
questions.answer: Globalization is often overstated and states remain powerful actors
questions.explanation: The skeptic perspective challenges claims that borders and governments have become irrelevant. It emphasizes historical comparisons and continuing state roles rather than denying all cross-border change.

questions.question: In global economic governance, the World Trade Organization (WTO) primarily:
options: Administers member-negotiated trade rules and dispute settlement procedures
Administers short-term balance-of-payments assistance
Finances long-term development projects
Coordinates a regional collective-defense alliance
questions.answer: Administers member-negotiated trade rules and dispute settlement procedures
questions.explanation: WTO members negotiate trade rules and use dispute settlement procedures. Vacancies prevent its Appellate Body from hearing appeals (checked November 2026), limiting the system's operation. Institutional mandate is distinct from guaranteed enforcement or a currently available appeal.

questions.question: Which hypothetical action illustrates soft power rather than coercion?
options: An import ban intended to impose economic costs
A naval deployment intended to deter an opponent
An asset freeze intended to pressure officials
A cultural exchange makes a country more attractive to audiences abroad
questions.answer: A cultural exchange makes a country more attractive to audiences abroad
questions.explanation: Attraction can influence how others view a country without imposing military or economic costs. A favorable image alone does not demonstrate that a foreign policy goal has been achieved.

questions.question: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is:
options: A regional convention binding only its ratifying states
A treaty creating direct criminal jurisdiction over all individuals
A Security Council decision authorizing a peacekeeping mission
A non-binding declaration adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948 establishing universal human rights standards
questions.answer: A non-binding declaration adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948 establishing universal human rights standards
questions.explanation: The UDHR is a declaration, not a treaty — it is not legally binding per se, but it has enormous moral authority and has shaped subsequent binding human rights treaties.

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement? The 'security dilemma' in international relations refers to:
options: One state's defensive actions making other states feel less secure, which can trigger escalation
A foreign conflict initiated to divert domestic discontent
A dispute generated by competing domestic bureaucratic budgets
Deliberate conquest driven by a desire for additional territory
questions.answer: One state's defensive actions making other states feel less secure, which can trigger escalation
questions.explanation: Defensive buildup can appear threatening to others, who then take countermeasures. Mutual insecurity can therefore escalate without either side initially intending aggression; escalation is not inevitable.

questions.question: An analyst focuses on how the distribution of power among states shapes a crisis, rather than on leaders or domestic groups. Which level of analysis is this?
options: Individual leaders' beliefs
Domestic political institutions
Systemic level
Bureaucratic rivalry inside a ministry
questions.answer: Systemic level
questions.explanation: The systemic level examines the structure of the international system and the distribution of power among states; individual and domestic levels examine actors within states.

questions.question: Define comparative advantage and distinguish it from absolute productivity.
questions.answer: Comparative advantage is production at a lower opportunity cost. A country can have it in a good even if another country produces more of both goods with the same resources.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): lower opportunity cost relative to the trading partner (0.5), and a correct distinction from output per resource or absolute advantage (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. A correct numerical illustration may supply the distinction.

questions.question: Constructivist IR theory argues that the interests of states are:
options: Given primarily by material capabilities and geography
Socially constructed through interaction, ideas, and shared norms
Derived solely from absolute economic size
Fixed by regime labels regardless of social interaction
questions.answer: Socially constructed through interaction, ideas, and shared norms
questions.explanation: Constructivists (e.g., Wendt) hold that identities and interests are not given by material factors but emerge from social interaction and the norms states develop in the international system.

questions.question: In this course, which level of analysis focuses on how the structure of the international system (anarchy, polarity) shapes state behavior?
options: Domestic institutional level
Domestic interest-group level
Individual level
System level
questions.answer: System level
questions.explanation: Anarchy and polarity describe features of the international system. Leaders' beliefs are individual factors, and institutions or organized interests within a state are domestic factors.

questions.question: Which description fits the agreed Responsibility to Protect commitment?
options: A general unilateral intervention entitlement after any rights violation
A development-aid obligation triggered by economic recession
A collective-defense duty responding to attacks on treaty allies
Protection from four specified atrocity categories, with peaceful means and Charter-based collective action
questions.answer: Protection from four specified atrocity categories, with peaceful means and Charter-based collective action
questions.explanation: R2P concerns genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. It prioritizes protection and peaceful measures. If peaceful means are inadequate and authorities manifestly fail, collective coercive action is considered case by case through the Security Council under the Charter, not as an unrestricted unilateral right.

questions.question: The Democratic Peace Theory predicts that:
options: Democracies rarely fight each other, though they do fight non-democracies
Shared authoritarian institutions best explain peace between democracies
Democratic institutions are unrelated to patterns of war
Democracies rarely fight any kind of state
questions.answer: Democracies rarely fight each other, though they do fight non-democracies
questions.explanation: The empirical pattern shows wars between established democracies are historically rare, while democracies do engage in wars with non-democratic states.

questions.question: A device is assembled through stages in four countries. What does this most directly illustrate?
options: A cross-border production chain
Production concentrated within a domestic vertical supply chain
A trade barrier preventing a component from crossing any border
A monetary arrangement setting one shared interest rate
questions.answer: A cross-border production chain
questions.explanation: Production stages linked across borders illustrate economic globalization. The diagram alone does not establish who receives most of the value or which labor rules are enforced.

questions.question: A factory moves into an export industry while a nearby import-competing factory loses orders. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: Integration affects each sector in proportion to its population alone
Import competition is sufficient to determine the economy's entire net result
Integration can distribute gains and costs unevenly across groups
Export performance is sufficient to determine every worker's welfare
questions.answer: Integration can distribute gains and costs unevenly across groups
questions.explanation: Distributional effects differ by sector, skill, bargaining power and policy. The case illustrates possible uneven effects, not proof of a universal net outcome.

questions.question: Explain one possible tension between self-determination and state sovereignty, and state one limit on the claim.
questions.answer: A group's demand to choose its political status can conflict with an existing state's claim to territorial integrity. This does not establish an automatic general right of unilateral secession; the legal and historical context matters.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): political-status versus territorial-integrity tension (0.5), and a limit rejecting automatic secession or identifying context-dependent legal conditions (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. Do not require endorsement of a disputed claim.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes systemic and domestic-level explanations of war?
options: Systemic explanations examine internal bureaucracies; domestic explanations examine international anarchy
Systemic explanations focus on the international distribution of power; domestic explanations examine institutions and groups within states
Systemic explanations concern only international organizations; domestic explanations concern only public opinion
Systemic explanations examine leaders' personalities; domestic explanations examine interstate polarity
questions.answer: Systemic explanations focus on the international distribution of power; domestic explanations examine institutions and groups within states
questions.explanation: Systemic theories examine features of the international system such as the distribution of power. Domestic-level theories examine institutions, interest groups, and other conditions within states; either lens may leave part of a case unexplained.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes treaty obligations from permanent Security Council membership?
options: A treaty's rules and party status determine its obligations; a permanent seat is not a general treaty exemption
Permanent-seat status is the legal test for NPT nuclear-weapon classification
NPT classification determines permanent Security Council membership
The UN Charter automatically applies every treaty to all member states
questions.answer: A treaty's rules and party status determine its obligations; a permanent seat is not a general treaty exemption
questions.explanation: Seat status and treaty obligations are different legal questions. In the NPT example, Article IX supplies a historical classification and obligations depend on applicable treaty provisions, not a Charter seat-based weapons ban.

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement? A collective action problem arises when:
options: Individual incentives make it difficult for a group to achieve a shared goal
Actors disagree over the boundary between two states
A state has several ministries with different administrative titles
A leader's private beliefs differ from advisers' beliefs
questions.answer: Individual incentives make it difficult for a group to achieve a shared goal
questions.explanation: A shared benefit can be underprovided when each actor prefers others to bear its cost. Rules, monitoring or incentives may improve cooperation but do not guarantee it.

questions.question: A government restricts trade and freezes assets to impose costs on another state. Which tool is illustrated?
options: Military hard power
Economic coercive statecraft
Diplomatic recognition withdrawal
Humanitarian intervention
questions.answer: Economic coercive statecraft
questions.explanation: Trade restrictions and asset freezes use economic leverage to impose costs. They are distinct from armed force, withdrawal of diplomatic recognition and attraction-based soft power; their effectiveness needs separate evidence.

questions.question: Which institution provides financing to member countries facing balance-of-payments problems?
options: OECD
World Bank
International Monetary Fund (IMF)
WTO
questions.answer: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
questions.explanation: The IMF lends to address balance-of-payments pressures. That role differs from development-project financing by the World Bank or administration of trade rules by the WTO; lending does not guarantee a crisis is resolved.

questions.question: An account explains a conflict through military bureaucracies and interest-group pressure. Which level is central?
options: Individual psychological level
Cross-border cultural-attraction mechanism
Domestic/state level
Systemic distribution-of-power level
questions.answer: Domestic/state level
questions.explanation: Institutions and organized groups within a state are domestic-level factors. Leader psychology is individual; the international distribution of capabilities is systemic.

questions.question: Use collective-action reasoning to explain why states can struggle to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions.
questions.answer: Mitigation produces shared benefits, while action has costs to individual states. A state may hope to benefit from others' reductions without contributing, creating a free-rider incentive.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): shared benefits with individual costs (0.5) and explanation of free riding or resulting underprovision (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. A clear mechanism earns credit without naming a theorist; the label alone earns at most 0.5.

questions.question: Which hypothetical action uses attraction rather than coercion?
options: A military threat pressures a neighboring government
An import restriction imposes costs on a trading partner
An asset freeze pressures named officials
A cultural exchange builds interest and trust among audiences abroad
questions.answer: A cultural exchange builds interest and trust among audiences abroad
questions.explanation: Soft power operates through attraction and perceived legitimacy. Cultural exchange may build favorable attitudes, but a policy effect requires evidence; sanctions and military threats are coercive tools.

questions.question: Why can an international court have legal jurisdiction yet still struggle to enforce an arrest?
options: Jurisdiction automatically supplies a court with a national police command
Practical noncooperation proves the court never had legal competence
It can depend on state cooperation and face political obstacles to carrying out its orders
A valid arrest order proves cooperation has already occurred
questions.answer: It can depend on state cooperation and face political obstacles to carrying out its orders
questions.explanation: Jurisdiction is legal competence under applicable rules; enforcement is practical implementation. The ICC lacks its own police and relies on cooperation. Political power can obstruct enforcement without itself deciding jurisdiction.

questions.question: The 'diversionary war' theory suggests military conflict may be initiated to:
options: Distract domestic audiences from internal political problems
Fulfill treaty obligations
Test new military technology
Acquire natural resources from weaker states
questions.answer: Distract domestic audiences from internal political problems
questions.explanation: Diversionary theory proposes that leaders facing domestic political pressure (economic crisis, scandal) may initiate international conflict to rally public support and shift attention outward.

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement? 'Transformationalists' in the globalization debate argue that:
options: Globalization consists chiefly of trade volumes rather than changes in governance
Global markets render state authority increasingly irrelevant
Contemporary integration is overstated and states remain largely as before
Globalization is fundamentally reshaping state power and sovereignty without necessarily eliminating them
questions.answer: Globalization is fundamentally reshaping state power and sovereignty without necessarily eliminating them
questions.explanation: Transformationalists emphasize deep, uneven changes in governance and how state authority is exercised. They do not simply average two positions or predict that all states inevitably disappear.

questions.question: Which category can fall within ICC subject-matter jurisdiction when the other legal conditions are met?
options: Claims concerning diplomatic recognition of governments
Genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity attributed to individuals
Maritime boundary claims between states
Trade disputes between sovereign states
questions.answer: Genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity attributed to individuals
questions.explanation: The ICC concerns individual criminal responsibility for specified crimes, including genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression under distinct conditions. Subject matter alone is insufficient: territorial/personal, temporal and admissibility conditions also matter, and national proceedings have priority when genuinely undertaken.

questions.question: In international-relations analysis, a multipolar distribution of power means:
options: Capabilities are distributed equally among every state
Several states hold substantial power relative to one another
One state holds a predominant share of major capabilities
Two states dominate major strategic capabilities
questions.answer: Several states hold substantial power relative to one another
questions.explanation: Multipolarity describes a system with several major centers of power; it is an analytical category rather than a claim that a particular current system has a settled classification.

questions.question: Give one liberal-institutionalist approach to a shared international problem and explain its proposed mechanism.
questions.answer: States could create an agreement with reporting and monitoring rules, reducing uncertainty about others' actions and supporting repeated cooperation. Other institution-based approaches with an explained mechanism are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): an institution, agreement or rule-based approach (0.5), and a mechanism such as information, monitoring or reciprocity (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. Cooperation is a possibility, not a guaranteed result.
